science.description: Eczema causes itchy, inflamed rashes on the skin Evgeniia Gordeeva/Getty Images Over a third of people with moderate to severe eczema taking part in a clinical trial have seen their skin completely or almost completely clear up after taking an experimental pill for four months. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected. “It definitely looks promising,” says Gayle Ross at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. Read more Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13. Advertisement In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is effective , it has had limited uptake in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage. Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter In the clinical trial , 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks. Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average 72 per cent reduction in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared to 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial. “These results exceeded our expectations,” said Terence Rooney , the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a webcast on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end. “It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross. Signs of unrest began in late October 2026. On October 27, seismic sensors recorded a sharp uptick in activity, and Japan’s Meteorological Agency reported that the first photographs of the eruption were captured. Soon after, sensors on several satellites began to capture an array of observations. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured the left image on October 26, when the coast was still quiet. On November 11, Landsat 9 got its first clear view of the land the submarine volcano has built (right). A shortwave-infrared signature, a sign of the eruption’s heat, is shown in orange. A faint gray volcanic plume drifts southeast of the vent, and a streak of floating pumice stretches across the water in the same direction. A false-color backscatter radar image from the NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite offered an even earlier look at the eruption. On October 28, despite heavy cloud cover, the radar detected a large disturbance in the water in the same area that erupted in December 2023. When the clouds cleared in early November, the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors on NASA and NOAA satellites also captured signs of the ongoing eruption’s volcanic plumes and infrared signature . Japan’s Coast Guard released a report on November 16 confirming the formation of new land connected to the pre-existing beach. The eruption appears to have added roughly 50 hectares (125 acres) of new beach, about the area of 90 American football fields. That would enlarge the island by about 1.7 percent. The new land adjoins the southeast beach where American troops landed on February 19, 1945, beginning one of the bloodiest battles in the history of the U.S. Marines. The location of the eruption is no surprise to scientists. In addition to the 2023 eruption off the southeast coast, Iwo Jima had an eruption off its west coast in August 2025, said Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. science.title: Will astronauts farm on the moon? Scientists successfully grow potatoes in simulated lunar dust
science.description:
Julian Dossett is a freelance writer living in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He primarily covers the rocket industry and space exploration and, in addition to science writing, contributes travel stories to New Mexico Magazine. In 2022 and 2024, his travel writing earned IRMA Awards. Previously, he worked as a staff writer at CNET. He graduated from Texas State University in San Marcos in 2011 with a B.A. in philosophy. He owns a large collection of sci-fi pulp magazines from the 1960s.

It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon. To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal. "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement . "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon." To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith , the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. The moon contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions. The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil. Oregon State University researchers David Handy and Aymeric Goyer studying potatoes grown in lunar regolith. (Image credit: Aymeric Goyer/David Handy/OSU) "We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, said in the same statement. The idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth. NASA funding supported this research.

science.description:
Alan Bradley is an experienced tech and culture writer with more than 20 years covering gaming, tech, and hardware. He has served as commerce director and in senior editorial roles at major publications. His work has appeared in Rolling Stone, U.S. News & World Report, PCMag, TechRadar, GamesRadar+, CNET, Live Science, Variety, and many other outlets. Alan is also a novelist—his debut novel, the urban fantasy The Sixth Borough, is available now.

Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics . The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation , the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut. Not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game. There was even Space Jam 's alien basketball game for the fate of the planet, though the gravity-defying antics there come from cartoon shenanigans rather than a zero-g playing field. As humanity edges closer to colonizing our neighbors through projects like the Artemis Program and its ambition to establish habitats on the moon, our imaginations have to expand to encompass not only how we'll live in space but also how we'll play. The rules change when gravity disappears (Image credit: Zero-G) We rarely think about it in an Earth context, but every sport is heavily influenced by gravity. It defines how balls arc, how quickly players can move, and even how we orient ourselves in play spaces. Remove the gravity, and all of those assumptions and mechanics evaporate as well. "First of all, in zero g, Isaac Newton will win every time," Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, told Space. Les is a physicist with over 35 years of experience working at Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, as well as a science fiction author. "'For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction,'" quotes Johnson. "This is very difficult to simulate in real life due to gravity; special effects often try to compensate. With today’s AI and green screens, it can actually look good on screen." In a microgravity scenario, the concept of up and down is no longer relevant. Suddenly, the playing field expands from a single, fixed plane to a fully three-dimensional space that includes height. (Image credit: Netflix) Momentum is also a completely different beast. Instead of being able to quickly stop and pivot the way you can during terrestrial sports, once you start moving in microgravity, you keep going until something stops you. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 23, 2015: Blue Origin sticks 1st-ever rocket landing from space with its suborbital New Shepard rocket
science.description: null On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever. After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground . This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history. The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste. (Image credit: Blue Origin) Why it mattered Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit. The company's triple-core Falcon Heavy boosters can also land vertically and its massive Starship megarocket can even return to the launch site to be caught by giant metal arms. But in the end, Blue Origin did it first. Blue Origin's New Shepard booster landing kicked off an era of vertical launch and vertical landings for rockets that continues to this day. It may have even outlasted the New Shepard rocket. Since that first landing, Blue Origin has launched 17 suborbital astronaut flights with New Shepard, and 21 more uncrewed flights for a total of 38 missions between April 2015 and 2026. The company reused its New Shepard boosters repeatedly (though it did lose one during an uncrewed launch after a technical issue.) But in January 2026, the company announced a pause in New Shepard flights for two years so that it could focus on moon lander projects. But Blue Origin did not abandon rocket landings. Indeed, the company's success with New Shepard led it to build vertical landing into its larger orbital rocket, New Glenn, which made its first successful landing 2025 — nearly 10 years after that first touchdown. Blue Origin has since reflown a New Glenn booster , and is developing a new rocket engine called Northstar for even better performance. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

science.title: NASA Seeks Partners to Design First Nuclear Reactor for the Moon
science.description: Artist’s concept of a nuclear fission power system on the Moon’s surface. Credit: NASA NASA is seeking industry partners to develop and test the first nuclear reactor designed to provide electricity on the Moon, a major step toward establishing a sustained human presence on the lunar surface. Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1) will be a small fission power system that will generate 20 kilowatts of electricity, enough to power approximately 16 average U.S. households annually on Earth. For NASA’s plans for a Moon Base , that energy could support future habitats, communications systems, rovers, scientific instruments, and other essential infrastructure. NASA aims to have a launch-ready system by 2030 and operate it on the Moon for at least five years after deployment. Unlike solar power, which depends on sunlight, a nuclear reactor can generate electricity continuously, including during the Moon’s approximately two-week-long nights. This capability will enable future lunar operations, particularly in locations where sunlight is limited or unavailable. “This request for proposals represents an important step forward as NASA partners with industry to establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface,” said Brian Giblin, NASA’s Lunar Reactor-1 program manager. “A reliable source of safe and abundant energy will be vital to future exploration of the lunar and Martian surface. Space nuclear systems will provide continuous power to NASA assets in any environment without dependency on sunlight.” NASA’s Space Power and Reactor Capabilities Request for Proposals incorporates feedback received after the agency released a draft proposal in August and hosted an industry day in September at the Ohio Aerospace Institute in Cleveland. The solicitation requires that the reactor must meet Department of Energy (DOE) safety standards for nuclear operations. While the primary purpose of the Request for Proposals is to advance the technology, testing, and flight design of LR-1, NASA may issue additional task orders to support the development of other space nuclear power systems. Proposals are due by Dec. 21. Nuclear power will be increasingly important to NASA’s space exploration ambitions. Lunar nights last about 14 Earth days, while dust storms on Mars can block sunlight for months. Farther from the Sun, solar power becomes progressively less effective. Nuclear systems offer a reliable source of electricity in these challenging environments. LR-1 is managed by the agency’s Space Reactors Division in partnership with the Department of Energy. The division is also responsible for the development of NASA’s Space Reactor‑1 (SR-1) Freedom. Scheduled to launch in 2028, SR-1 Freedom will deliver three SkyFall helicopters to Mars and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion, which uses electricity generated by a nuclear reactor to power spacecraft propulsion systems. science.description: null NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface. While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years. In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life. NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency. NASA's Curiosity rover captured a close-up view of unusual, disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in Martian bedrock using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI) on Nov. 7, 2026 (Sol 5067). The thin, flattened formations resemble tiny potato chips. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) Curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day , or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis. Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape. Data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. science.title: The remains of a long-dead volcano on Mars | Space photo of the day for Nov. 23, 2026
science.description: null An image of Tharsis Tholus, a volcano on the surface of Mars, produced by ESA's Mars Express orbiter. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet. What is it? The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible new imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus. This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera. Even as old and worn as it is, the Martian volcano stands at around 4.97 miles (8 kilometers) tall which is comparable to some of the highest peaks in the Himalayan mountains. Despite its impressive height, it's still only about a medium-sized volcano for Mars, which is home much more impressively-sized volcanoes. For example, the planet's largest volcano Olympus Mons measures in at roughly 13.2 miles high (21.3 kilometers). Tharsis Tholus, a volcano on the surface of Mars, as seen by ESA's Mars Express orbiter. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) Why is it incredible? While Tharsis Tholus might not be the tallest volcano on Mars, it is incredibly steep. It is steeper than Mauna Kea in Hawaii on Earth. To fully showcase the volcano's structure and topography in 3D, researchers actually exaggerated the vertical scale in this image, ESA reported . In addition to being steep and fairly tall, the volcano also has an interesting history. You can see that it is speckled with what look like small holes which are actually craters created by impacts from objects like asteroids. The volcano's current, unique shape is a combined effort by these impacts, environmental factors causing erosion and warping and ancient lava flows that left behind built-up material. The observations by Mars Express also reveals cracks and other imperfections in the volcano. All of these details might seem like superficial bits of detail, however every small crater, every lumpy cliffside and every worn down surface hides information about the planet's past. By studying features like volcanoes on Mars, researchers can piece together what the planet may have looked like in its ancient past. How active was this volcano? How did it interact with the landscape around it? Observations like this can hold the answers.

science.title: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
science.description: A closing plenary session at the COP31 climate summit on 22 November AP Photo/Khalil Hamra/Alamy A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels. Read more Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet? The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency. Advertisement But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia. Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels” , but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates. Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.” Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change. Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”. science.title: What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?
science.description:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service. However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been. So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure? Last of the Soviet space explorers Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June. The stakes were almost immediately raised as Phobos 2 arrived in orbit around Mars on Jan. 30, 1989 , when one of the probe's three onboard flight system processors was found to have gone offline, with another already experiencing technical issues. Over the course of the next several weeks, Phobos 2 was able to overcome some of these setbacks and successfully began sending useful scientific data about the Martian environment back to Earth. By March, all the probe's science instruments appeared to be functioning normally, and despite the earlier loss of one of its processors, the remaining two had continued to facilitate control of the spacecraft by its Soviet ground control team.
